Short answer: How this Hugo blog uses Aamu.app as a headless CMS with database rows, Docs content, GraphQL, generated Markdown, and static publishing.
This blog uses Aamu.app as a headless CMS: post metadata lives in a Database, article text is written in Docs, and a build script fetches both to generate a Hugo site.
Writers edit Docs, editors manage publication status and metadata in the Database, and a static host serves the generated HTML.
What we are buildingThe basic flow looks like this:
Aamu Docs -> BlogPost row in Aamu Database -> GraphQL API + Docs API -> Hugo content files -> static blogThe Database row is used for the structured parts of the post: title, slug, author, publish date, status, tags, hero image, and the linked Doc. The Doc is the source of truth for the article body. Hugo is used only at build time to create the public site.
You can see the source code for this blog at https://github.com/AamuApp/aamu-blog.
Why use Aamu.app as a headless CMS?A traditional CMS can be useful, but it also becomes another product to maintain. If your team already works in Aamu, using Aamu as the CMS keeps writing, metadata, project work, and internal knowledge close together.
This approach is useful when you want:
a familiar writing experience through Aamu Docs,
structured blog metadata in an Aamu Database,
a public site that is static, fast, and easy to host,
a build pipeline that can run on your own server, CI, or a static hosting service,
GraphQL access to the database rows, and
Docs API access to the actual article HTML.
The ingredientsFor a setup like this blog, you need:
an Aamu Database created from the aamu-blog template,
Aamu Docs for writing the post bodies,
a BlogPost table where each row stores post metadata and links to a Doc,
a Person table for authors,
an API key that can read the database and the linked Docs,
Hugo for generating the static site, and
some deployment target such as Netlify, Cloudflare Pages, Vercel, or your own server.
Create the blog databaseCreate a database in Aamu.app with the provided aamu-blog template. The template gives you the basic shape for a blog: a BlogPost table and a Person table.
The BlogPost table is for posts. It stores fields such as title, slug, description, publish date, status, tags, author, hero image, and the Doc reference. The Person table is for post authors.
Write the article in Aamu Docs and link it through the BlogPost row’s Doc field.
Write posts in Aamu DocsCreate a new Doc for the article and write the post there. This gives you the normal Aamu Docs writing experience: rich text, headings, lists, links, images, collaboration, snapshots, and source views.
When the post is ready, create or update the matching BlogPost row in the database. Set the title, slug, author, publish date, tags, hero image, and status. Then select the Doc in the row's Doc field.
That Doc is the article source. The build script reads the BlogPost rows through GraphQL and then fetches the linked Doc through the Docs API. If the Doc has HTML content, that HTML becomes the Hugo post body.
What about the Body field?The Body field is only for manually written or copy-pasted HTML. It is useful as a fallback, or if you really want to manage the post body as raw HTML in the database row.
Do not use the Body field as the normal Doc workflow. In the current Aamu.app UI, you cannot attach a Doc to the Body field. If you want the post to be written in Docs, link the Doc through the row's Doc field instead.
Configure the API keyThe build script needs to read published BlogPost rows and fetch the linked Docs. This is done with an API key stored as an environment variable on the machine or CI job that builds the site.
For this blog repository, the useful environment variables are:
API_KEY=your_api_key AAMU_DB_ID=your_database_id AAMU_API_BASE_URL=https://your-aamu-host.example # Optional, depending on your setup: DOCS_API_KEY=your_docs_api_key AAMU_PROJECT_ID=your_project_id GRAPHQL_ENDPOINT=https://api.aamu.app/api/v1/graphql/Keep API keys on the server side. Do not commit them to Git, do not publish them in frontend JavaScript, and do not paste them into public examples. The static site can be public, but the build credentials should stay private.
Build the Hugo siteThe blog repository contains a build script that does the content sync before Hugo runs. The basic command is:
node build-with-graphql.js hugo --minifyOr as one command:
node build-with-graphql.js && hugo --minifyThe script does a few things:
queries the BlogPost rows through the GraphQL API,
filters for published posts,
detects the Doc field in the BlogPost schema,
fetches the linked Doc through the Docs API,
uses the Doc HTML as the post body,
downloads images into the Hugo post folder,
writes Hugo-compatible content/posts/.../index.md files, and
lets Hugo create the final static site.
The generated Hugo content files are build artifacts. The source of truth is the Aamu Database row plus the linked Doc.
Deployment optionsThere are several reasonable ways to publish the generated static site.
Static hosting serviceYou can use a service such as Netlify, Cloudflare Pages, Vercel, or another static host. In that setup, configure the environment variables in the hosting service and use the build command above. A build hook can trigger a new build when content changes.
Your own serverYou can also build on your own machine or server and serve the generated files with Nginx or another web server. The official Aamu blog has used a Git-based deployment flow with a bare repository and a post-receive hook. That works well if you like controlling the server yourself, but it is only one option.
CI pipelineA third option is a CI job. The job checks out the blog repository, sets the Aamu API environment variables, runs the build, and uploads the generated public/ directory to your hosting target.
Next stepsIf you want to build a blog like this:
Fork or clone AamuApp/aamu-blog.
Create an Aamu Database from the aamu-blog template.
Create a Person row for the author.
Create a Doc for your first post.
Create a BlogPost row and link the Doc in the row's Doc field.
Add the API environment variables to your build environment.
Run node build-with-graphql.js && hugo --minify.
Deploy the generated public/ directory.
After editing a Doc or its post metadata, rebuild the site to publish the changes.

Short answer: Aamu.app is an all-in-one productivity tool
Aamu.app brings tasks, Docs, databases, customer support, communication and code into one project-based workspace.
Company Brain lets AI retrieve context from the workspace according to the signed-in user’s permissions.
Start with one workflow, then connect the documents, conversations and data that explain the work.
One workspace, one mental modelProjects, tasks, Docs, meetings, databases, forms, files, email, Helpdesk tickets, newsletters, design work, presentations, external applications, and code are not isolated categories in real life. They describe the same customers, products, decisions, deadlines, and responsibilities. Aamu keeps those relationships close instead of forcing the team to reconstruct them through integrations.
The interface follows the same principle. Once a team learns the main patterns for projects, navigation, editors, comments, permissions, and activity, that understanding carries across the workspace. Aamu is useful as a focused task and knowledge workspace on day one, and it can grow into the operational home for a whole team.
Your whole company is on the same pageA customer conversation can lead to a task. The task can point to the Doc that explains the decision. A meeting can record the discussion and action items. A database row can hold the structured customer or product data. The Activity feed can show what changed and link people back to the source.
Tasks turn intention into accountable workAamu Tasks supports lists, Kanban boards, calendar-oriented planning, reminders, comments, files, timers, custom fields, and statuses in the same workflow. Tasks live next to the information that gives them meaning: a support ticket can become follow-up work, a Doc can explain why the work matters, and a meeting can produce action items.
Tasks can also be created through forms, database automations, API integrations and AI commands.
Docs and databases give the work memoryAamu Docs are collaborative documents for plans, decisions, internal knowledge, specifications, meeting material, and publishing. Real-time editing, comments, snapshots, links, and sharing keep knowledge usable as it develops. Docs can be linked from tasks, tickets, database rows, and other workspace objects, and selected Docs can provide carefully maintained context for Company Brain.
Databases hold the structured side of the company. They can power a CRM, content workflow, internal tool, lightweight application, or public site. Tables support different ways to work with the same data, including grid and row views, linked records, activity history, and automations. New database dashboards can turn the data into a team-facing view with tables, cards, summaries, and charts.
Forms can write submissions directly into a database, while GraphQL, the REST API, API keys, and webhooks make the data available to external applications and automations. This blog demonstrates the model: its metadata lives in an Aamu Database, its articles are written in Aamu Docs, and an external build reads both through the API.
Communication belongs beside the workEmail, Helpdesk tickets, Live chat, video meetings, team chat, and newsletters are included because communication is not separate from operations. A customer question may reveal a bug, a missing document, a product request, or a process that needs to change.
Meetings can produce notes and tasks. Aamu's meeting AI can transcribe conversation with speaker information and update live notes containing summaries, decisions, topics, action items, and mentioned references. Support and email assistants can prepare drafts for review, while sending remains an explicit human-controlled action. Newsletters can be written and sent close to the source material and the team responsible for it.
Slides, design, Git, and My AppsAamu Slides brings spatial presentations into the project workspace. Decks are connected to projects and can be opened from Aamu, while deck creation can appear in the Activity feed. Team AI settings can also provide the Slides assistant with the team's configured provider without exposing provider credentials to the presentation application.
Penpot provides design and prototyping, and Git keeps repositories, issues, commits, pull requests, and code-related discussion close to product work. The newer My Apps area extends the workspace to team-owned applications: an external service can synchronize its items and activity into Aamu, use scoped API access, and open with Aamu authentication. The external app remains the source of its own data, while the team gets a connected entry point, permissions, and activity in the workspace.
Company Brain: AI with the whole pictureCompany Brain gives Aamu AI a permission-aware view across the workspace. Ask from Launch AI or mention @ai. It can retrieve context from tasks, Docs, meetings and transcripts, Forms, file metadata, Databases and rows, Helpdesk tickets, Newsletters, projects, team members and the signed-in user’s own email.
That enables questions that do not fit inside a single app:
What did we decide about onboarding, and is there already a task for it?
What have we promised this customer?
Which meeting introduced the new deadline?
Where is the current process documented?
Do we already have structured data for this company?
Answers can link back to the original Aamu objects, so AI does not become a competing source of truth. It helps people find and understand the work; the task, Doc, meeting, ticket, or database row remains the source.
Permissions are part of retrieval. Company-level knowledge stays within the team, project information is limited to projects the person can access, and user-owned sources such as email have an additional owner check. The model is given only the context the signed-in person is allowed to see. Teams can configure their AI provider and model at team level, including supported hosted providers and OpenAI-compatible local endpoints.
AI should work inside the workflowAI can help write Docs, answer workspace questions, turn comments into actions, summarize meetings and draft customer replies.
AI commands can turn natural-language instructions into concrete workspace operations across tasks, Docs, Forms, meetings, Helpdesk, Email, files, databases, rows, and automations. Human control remains visible: generated support or email replies appear as drafts for review, and reversible content work is separate from actions such as sending a message or changing important data.
Keep control of your dataBringing work together should not mean giving up control. Aamu supports incremental daily backups to your own S3-compatible storage, data import and export, scoped API keys, and webhooks. APIs make major workspace features available to integrations and AI-assisted automation, while permissions and explicit scopes keep access bounded.
Where to startStart with Tasks or with one workflow that is currently fragmented: customer support, product planning, a knowledge base, a content process, a database-backed form, or a presentation workflow. Bring the work and its immediate context into Aamu. Then connect the Docs, conversations, meetings, data, and applications that explain it.
